Their sessions started before this change have their transcripts in the directory they ran under, and the first launch in the worktree, a resume or a fresh one, records that directory (D2).
They keep it until the operator changes the record.

Rationale: an orch and a dobby are resumed across restarts, and a resume needs the session's transcript, which only its own directory holds.
A switch on each fresh start would split one worktree's sessions over two directories, and the readers of D6 read one directory per worktree.

### D8 — A usage limit is reported and waited out, never moved to another account

A session that hits its account's limit is handled as today: the engine reports the limit and its reset, and the orch watcher waits it out (`internal/orchengine/usagelimit.go`).
Lym does not move a worktree or a session to another account.

Rationale: a session's history is in its account's config directory, so a session moved to another account cannot resume.
The pick's headroom check keeps new worktrees off an account near a limit, which covers the case the move would serve.

### D9 — Tests run on fake config directories; a manual check runs on the operator's second account

Automated tests use fake config directories under the test's temporary directory, each with an empty `.credentials.json` where the test needs a logged-in account.
They feed the status line verb fake JSON on stdin.
No automated test reads a real account or calls Claude.

The second account is wired for the manual check this way, by the operator, once before landing:
the operator logs it in with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=<dir> claude` and `/login`;
links `<dir>/plugins` to `~/.claude/plugins`, so lym's deploy, which syncs plugins into `~/.claude` alone, updates both accounts;
links the user-level instruction file and settings from `~/.claude` as wanted;
and lists both accounts with `lym config claude --layer machine`.
The check then starts two task runs and confirms each worktree's record names an account, a session's transcript lands in that account's `projects/`, and the hub's usage directory gains a file per used account.

Rationale: the board says the build is tested against fake directories and a fake usage source unless a real second account is wired, and that the task states how it is wired.

## Constraints

- `PATTERN-shuttle-provider-seam`: `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, the credentials file name, the status line verb's input shape and the pick live in `internal/shuttleengine/claudeengine`.
  A verb wired outside it reaches it only through `internal/shuttleengines`.
- `PATTERN-config-layers`: the new key is classified in the module's `ConfigSpec` in the same change, as `CategoryMachine`; it is a new key, so no reinterpretation is needed.
- `PATTERN-lym-files`: every new path, the worktree's record, the counter file and the usage directory, is named in `internal/lymdirs`; lock paths come from `internal/lock`.
- `PATTERN-tolerant-records`: the record, the counter file and the usage files are JSON read tolerantly and rewritten through `internal/state`.
- `PATTERN-cli-cobra`: the status line verb is a cobra command under the one root.

## Auto-mode assumptions

- A worktree's account is sticky while its directory exists, the prime's and beams' included (D2, D7).
  The operator changes it by writing the record with another directory, which a record holding only its `config_dir` key does, the record being read tolerantly;
  a removed record is written again with the directory that holds the transcripts of the worktree's resumable sessions, so removal alone moves only a worktree with none.
- The status line does not chain to the operator's own command (D5).

## Open risks

- The headroom view and the share are per hub (D3), and this machine runs several hubs; a hub that rarely uses an account can pick it while another hub has spent it, until its own session sees the figures.
- Claude Code may change the status line input's field names; the verb then writes nothing and every account reads as having headroom, so the pick falls back to the weights alone.

## Acceptance criteria

- D1: a `claude.accounts` list in the machine layer loads with each entry's name, directory, weight and windows; a duplicate name, a relative path, two entries naming one directory after cleaning, a non-positive weight, an unknown window or a threshold outside 1 to 100 is refused.
- D1: a non-empty `claude.accounts` from a tracked `claude.yaml` is refused, also when the machine file lists accounts, and the refusal names `lym config claude --layer machine`.
- D1: with `claude.accounts` empty and no record, a session's launch command and resume command neither set nor unset `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, and a resume launch writes no record.
- D2: a second session started in a worktree after the first uses the recorded directory, without a new pick.
- D2: a record whose account was removed from the list, its directory still present, is kept and its directory exported.
- D2: a fresh launch with a record whose directory is gone, and no transcript of the worktree in any known directory, picks again and replaces the record;
  a resume launch with such a record is refused, naming the directory;
  with `claude.accounts` empty, a fresh launch and a resume launch with such a record are both refused, naming the directory and the way forward, and neither exports nor writes anything.
- D2: a resume launch in a worktree with no record, with `claude.accounts` listing an account, its transcript in the default directory, records the default directory and advances no count.
- D2: a fresh launch in a worktree with no record, whose resumable sessions' transcripts sit in the default directory, records the default directory and advances no count.
- D2: a fresh launch in a new worktree at a path whose earlier worktree left transcripts in the default directory, with no session of its own, picks.
- D2: a resume launch with no record, its transcript found in no known directory, writes no record.
- D2: a resume launch in a worktree with no record, with `claude.accounts` listing an account, its transcript under the `env` module's `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, records that directory.
- D2: a resume launch with no record, its transcript in a listed non-default account's directory, passes the resume check and records that directory.
- D2: a fresh launch in a prime whose orch state record names a session whose transcript is in the default directory records the default directory and makes no pick.
- D2: a fresh launch in a worktree with no record, whose only resumable session id sits in a PR-Review or sampler record, its transcript in the default directory and its shuttle run directory gone, records the default directory and makes no pick.
- D3: with weights 2 and 1 and both accounts eligible, six picks give the first account four and the second two, never two of the second in a row.
- D3: an account with a window at or above its threshold, its reset in the future, is passed over; the same account with its reset passed is eligible.
- D3: an account whose directory has no `.credentials.json` is never picked, by the weights or the fallback; with none having one, the launch fails naming the directories.
- D3: with every candidate short, the pick takes the candidate whose latest blocking reset is earliest;
  a candidate with two blocking windows is judged by the later of them, and a tie goes to the earlier entry.
- D3: an account added to a list with existing counts has its count set to the lowest count over weight among the other accounts listed at the last pick under an unchanged weight, times its weight, never left at zero;
  an account whose weight was lowered, and a re-added account with a kept count, has its count set to that value the same way, whether that raises or lowers it; an account listed throughout under one weight is never changed.
- D3: after a re-added account's count is set, or a reweighted one's, it is picked only while its count over weight is no higher than that of every other eligible account,
  and an account that gained weight takes no pick before its count over weight reaches the lowest of the others.
- D3: two sessions starting at once in one worktree with no record end with one record and one counter increment.
- D3: a resume and a fresh launch starting at once in one worktree with no record end with one record.
- D4: a session in a worktree whose recorded directory is not the default gets a launch command and a resume command that export `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` as that directory, after any `env` module value.
- D4: a worktree whose recorded directory is `~/.claude` gets a launch command that unsets `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`.
- D4: a session opened with `lym shuttle open` in a worktree recorded on a non-default directory gets launch and resume lines that export `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` as that directory.
- D4: a tmux server spawned from a process whose environment holds `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` carries none of it.
- D5: the status line verb, given an account name, its directory and input with both windows, writes that account's usage file with both windows' percentage and reset; given input without `rate_limits`, it writes nothing.
- D5: the verb given a name that does not match `[a-z0-9-]+`, a name no listed account has, or a directory other than the named entry's, writes nothing.
- D5: after a name moves to another directory, the first status line input for it replaces the stored windows whatever their resets.
- D5: a window with `used_percentage` outside 0 to 100, or with `resets_at` more than its window's length past now, is dropped, and the other window is written.
- D5: a stored window is replaced by one with a later reset or a higher percentage at the same reset, and kept against one with a lower percentage at the same reset or an earlier reset.
- D5: a session whose worktree's recorded directory is a listed account's gets session settings carrying the status line command with that entry's current name and directory, after the account was renamed in the list too;
  with no listed entry for the directory, the settings carry none; an opened session's settings follow the same rule.
- D5: an account whose usage file lacks a window it lists, or has none, reads as having headroom in that window.
- D6: the engine's live-session transcript read, resume check and plugin lookup for a worktree recorded on a fake directory find the files in that directory and not under `~/.claude`.
- D6: the resume check refuses a resume of a session registered as held by a live process only in a listed non-default account's registry, also when the check resolved another directory, and passes one whose registry entry there is dead.
- D6: the liveness read of a session id registered only under a fake account directory finds the session.
- D6: a session registered dead in a listed account's registry, the default directory holding no registry directory, reads dead; one registered alive in any known directory reads alive.
- D6: the session-end usage record of a session run on a listed non-default account carries its transcript's figures.
- D6: `tools/tokencount` counts a landed run's sessions under every known directory, a listed non-default account's and the `env` module's included, with the run's worktree and record gone, and counts a session id found in two of them once.
- D6: a record reader built for a hub finds a session under a listed account's directory with the session's worktree and its record gone.
- D7: a prime or beam worktree's orch session and dobby session run under the worktree's recorded directory.
- D8: a session that hits a usage limit keeps its recorded `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` across the wait and its resume.
- Review: D9's manual check on the real second account is written in the task's landing notes with its outcome.

## Previous board body, to reuse

The board body of the cancelled Sketch, verbatim (headings lowered one level).

## Idea (operator, 2026-11-02)

Spread Claude usage over two accounts, so one account's limits are not the bottleneck: each worktree uses one of the accounts, chosen by a weight.
The weights are config, for example account A twice for each use of account B, so account A carries twice the load of B on average.

## Accounts of different plans (operator, 2026-11-03)

The accounts need not be of one plan: for example a Claude Ultra account beside a Max account with about half its usage.
The plans' limit windows differ too: the operator reports that Max has a five-hour window that Ultra lacks.
So a fixed weight alone is not enough: a Max account can hit its five-hour window while its weekly share is far from spent.

- The weight sets the long-run share, from each account's plan.
- The pick also reads each account's current headroom in every window it has, and passes over an account that is near or at a limit; an account with no five-hour window is never judged by one.
- The pick is more than a weight: the operator says an account's usage for the session window and the week can be read, so the pick reads both (operator, 2026-11-11).
- Lym today learns of a limit only when a pane shows the usage-limit message (`internal/shuttleengine/claudeengine/usagelimit.go`); reading an account's headroom before a pick is new, and the source is open: Claude Code's status line input, `/usage`, or lym's own transcript totals per config directory against a configured budget. Check what Claude Code exposes before choosing, and which of these gives the session and week figures.
- This was weighed against offloading to Codex (`codex-engine`): the two-account route keeps every agent on Claude's review quality and is far smaller to build, so it is the first route to quota relief (orch, 2026-11-03).

## Testing needs a second account (operator, 2026-11-11)

A test of the pick and the headroom reads needs a real second Claude account on the machine, which the operator provides.
Without it the Discussion and the build can be tested only against a fake config directory and a fake usage source.
The task that builds this states in its body how the second account is wired for the test.

## Seen (orch, 2026-11-02)

Lym cannot pick an account per worktree today.
`lym config claude` has no key for an account or a config directory, and a search of `internal/` found no use of `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, so every session runs under whichever account the machine is logged in to.

Claude Code is believed to keep an account's login in a config directory that the `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable selects.
That is not verified: check it against the Claude Code documentation before anything is built.

## Built since

`lym config env` (`0d155d1a`, landed 2026-11-03) holds per-machine environment variables that lym exports to every process it starts for the hub: gate tiers, Drift steps and agent session panes.
A pane receives them through the `PaneEnv` closure on reed's geometry, exported ahead of the strand's launch command and read afresh at each launch.
It refuses `PATH` and any `LYM_` name, and `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is allowed.

So a machine-wide `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` can be set today, which moves every session to one other account.
It is one value for the whole hub: the per-worktree pick, the weights and the headroom check below are still unbuilt.

Heddle's `claude-settings` target (`72390eb3`) is no source for the account: its entries live in the Bolt, which is pushed to GitHub, and account details never go into a file pushed to GitHub (operator, 2026-11-07); it also renders one file for every worktree, and the account must be chosen before Claude starts, through its environment.
The accounts and the pick stay machine-local.

## Design questions for a Discussion

- Config: a list of accounts, each with a name, a config directory, a weight and its limit windows, in the claude config; a machine-layer key, since the accounts belong to the machine.
- Choice: per worktree, never per session, so all of a run's sessions (writer, reviewers, fixers, driver) share one account.
  The pick is made once, when the worktree's first session starts, and recorded with the worktree so a resume, a re-attach and a hand pass keep it.
  With headroom in the pick, a deterministic hash of the slug no longer suffices: a persisted weighted counter that skips an account short of headroom is the candidate.
- Scope: the prime's orch and each beam's orch and dobby need a rule of their own, since they outlive a task run.
- A session spawn sets the chosen account's environment in one place in the claude engine's launch, so no caller sets it.
  The pane launch now already exports the `env` module's variables ahead of the launch command (`reedengine/panebin.go`); the account's variable would sit beside them, and its precedence over the module's is to be decided.
- A usage limit on one account: whether lym moves a worktree to the other account when one is limited, or only reports it; the first needs the session's history to be readable under the other account, which it is not by default.
- Cost and quota reports (`lym report`, `tokencount`) read transcripts per config directory, and would need to read both.

## Not in scope

Logging the accounts in, and whether the use is within the accounts' and the organisation's terms, which is the operator's to settle.

entries.title: Move a running task by hand-back and a fresh run, not a re-parent verb
entries.brief: The writer hands back what it knows, the run is cancelled, a new task under the new parent starts from that
entries.body:
## Seen

The study `docs/research/loom/reparent-running-task-2026-11-12.md` (commit `5e41ee2b`) finds that a verb moving a running task to another parent is feasible but wide:
two durable stores written by two modules with no atomic change, a narrow board write past the run lock,
an ancestry check on the new parent, and a cross-module tapestry run of its own.

## Idea (operator, 2026-11-15)

Moving a running task is rare, and a verb for it is clumsy for what it buys.
Instead, end the run and start a new one with more information:

1. The run's live writer writes everything it has learned to a hand-back file in its run records:
   what is done, the decisions taken, what is left, and where its commits are.
   The entry is held by the run and takes no body edit, so the file is the only place it can write.
2. The run is cancelled with `lym batten cancel`, which sets the entry back to `draft` and frees it.
   The archive tag keeps the run records, the hand-back and the commits, so the new run can read them.
3. The orch writes the hand-back into the entry's body, or into a new task under the new parent, and releases it.

What the design must settle:

- Whether the new run re-uses the old commits (a cherry-pick, which brings back the study's ancestry question) or only reads them.
- Whether this is a recipe step, a `lym batten` verb, or orch guidance alone.

The adopt redesign (`adopt-redesign`) has landed, and so has `run-fsm-tracked-records` (`27eefef6`, one run FSM over tracked records).
The rest of how run state moves is built by the members of the project `adopt-build-resplit`, still open (`push-before-act-takeover` among them).
Waits until those have landed.

entries.title: Merge the remaining adopt-build members into one design and split it again on what landed
entries.body:
Groups the entries filed from the Sketch `adopt-build-resplit`: transition-push-takeover, machine-registry-holds-catchup, adopt-foreground, leftover-pairs-teardown, hub-stop-all, machine-start-launchers, board-prints-root-beam.

## Why (operator, 2026-11-16)

Raddle split the Sketch `adopt-redesign` into the members of the beam `adopt-build` before any of them ran.
Two members have landed in the beam since, `orch-resume-own-session` and `run-fsm-tracked-records`,
and the operator has decided more since the split:
the orch resumes its own session on the same machine only, with no transcript mirror;
the orch stays up during an adopt hold;
the stop button, the restart launcher and the root-beam fix joined the beam.
The remaining members were cut for a state that no longer stands.
This entry merges every remaining member into one design, to be split again from scratch under raddle's split rules,
on what landed and what the operator decided.
Splitting, merging or reordering the parts is open, and so is moving a part out of the beam.

## Input

- The beam's branch as it stands, with the two landed members' code, such as `internal/runfsm`.
- The Sketch's decision record, under Bolt's `raddle/adopt-redesign`.
- The study `adopt-build-revision`, `docs/research/loom/adopt-build-revision-2026-11-16/report.md` on the beam's branch.
  Use its findings on what the landed members built and what each remaining part takes from them.
  Its proposed shape, each member kept and one added, was rejected by the operator: never take it as the split.
- The merged members' designs, below, as each stood when merged.

## Merged members

### push-before-act-takeover

Every transition pushes its records before the run acts, and a takeover entry in the run's records hands it over without replay.

Takes: runfsm's Act inputs and the batten record from run-fsm-tracked-records; fabricengine's PushPairAnchored, SpawnStatusPush, teardown-lock respawn, pushclassified's rejection path and ArchiveOwnerTips; boardengine's Sync, SpawnSync and pushOwnerCommit; statuscommit and sheddriver's records commit; landingshed's Finalize; runproc's End for a slug

Delivers: a shed transition that takes a gate admission, commits its records with the code tip it was made with and pushes records side first, code side after, before the next producer starts; an owed push retried on a backoff and shown in lym beam status, which tender's offline pause and resume intents also ride; the per-transition detached push and its teardown-lock respawn retired; synchronous Bolt writes for a run claim, a landing's done and an owner; Finalize pushing the parent branch before its transition and board done; a rejected records push that reads origin's record and hands over on another machine's takeover entry, archiving local tips and the local parent merge; the code-tip wait and its grace

Exports: the takeover entry type and its reader, tested with kit-written entries; the owed-push and code-tip facts runfsm's Act reads; fabricengine's records-first PushPairAnchored and its hand-over result

Packages, by the Sketch's estimate: fabricengine (about 1000 changed lines); battencli, sheddriver, loomcli, landingshed (about 200 each); boardengine, statuscommit (100 to 150); shedengine, beamcli, fabriccli, tendercli, tenderengine, pauserecord, pattern (under 60 each).

### bolt-holds-catch-up

A machine registry and holds in Bolt, the owner pause caller retired, and a catch-up from origin after an absence.

Takes: runfsm's Act rule, the synchronous Bolt writes, the takeover reader and hand-over and the owed-push facts from push-before-act-takeover; the subject-process end from orch-resume-own-session; boardengine's owner setter and OwnedElsewhere, machinename's former names, pauserecord's callers and SleepWatch, the dobby's loop and handover, battencli's origin-owed marker, pairteardown's local mode

Delivers: board.json's machines registry and holds list written only by boardengine's setter with a synchronous push; every machine-name comparison through the registry, OwnedElsewhere's callers in every package updated; lym machine name --forget-former; hold slug entries under the new pauserecord caller hold, read by every machine; the owner caller and its writers retired into hand_over with the subject-process end; the origin-owed marker retired; the catch-up from origin after a sleep, a dobby start or a hand pass, pushing owed commits, handing over runs owned elsewhere and removing their local pairs in local mode, the dobby's handover calling the subject-process end

Exports: boardengine's registry and hold types, setters and readers, OwnedElsewhere taking the registry, and the catch-up entry point adopt calls as its step 4

Packages, by the Sketch's estimate: boardengine (about 600 changed lines), dobbyengine (about 450); pauserecord, machinecli, orchcli, tenderengine, battencli, beamcli (100 to 150 each); tendercli, hibernateengine, adoptcli, machinename, loomcli, battenshed and a tail of small ones (under 60 each).

### adopt-foreground-leftovers

lym adopt runs in the foreground over pushed state, with --take-hold, and the dobby tears down or reports leftover pairs.

Takes: the holds, registry, catch-up and owner setter from bolt-holds-catch-up; the takeover entry type, its reader and the synchronous pushes from push-before-act-takeover; runfsm's states; adoptcli's fix loop, check, deploy, archives and here paths; the dobby's ended-run teardown and pairteardown

Delivers: lym adopt running hold, owner, pull, takeover, catch-up, deploy, workspace, check and green clear in the caller's process, re-runnable from tracked state, with the takeover entry writer and its rejected-push retry, and --take-hold denied to agents by a shell-guard row; the worker, adopt record and its readers, verdicts, pause step, the adopt and adopt-hold pause callers, --keep-local, --drop-local and --discard retired, with the upgrade's first read turning standing adopt entries into pause intents and one Bolt hold; the dobby tearing down landed and unkept cancelled pairs, listing kept pairs, writing kept-cancel records for pre-upgrade kept pairs, and tearing down idle orphans after the orphan grace; lym tender resume pushing no pair; the hub workspace file regenerated after each teardown

Exports: adopt's foreground step runner, the takeover entry writer and the orphan grace constant

Packages, by the Sketch's estimate: adoptcli (about 2650 changed lines), adoptrecord (about 400), dobbyengine (about 350); fabricengine, beamcli (about 150 each); orchcli, pauserecord, battencli, shellguard, tendercli, pairteardown, cmd/lym, pattern (under 80 each).

### prime-is-root-beam

The prime is the root beam: parent_beam names it, never empty.

Seen (operator, 2026-11-15): `lym board list` and `lym board get` give `parent_beam` empty for an entry whose nearest beam is the prime, and `lym board list --text` shows no `P0`,
while the board view and window titles show the prime as `P0`.
The prime is a beam, the root one; an empty value reads as "no beam".

- `parent_beam` names the root beam, as `P0` or its slug, for every entry under the prime, never empty.
- `lym board list --text` shows `P0` with the other projects, so every view of the board shows the same tree.
- Every reader of an empty `parent_beam` (orch role, dobby, board verbs) moves to the named root in the same change.

### hub-stop-button

A stop button in the prime orch session that takes the whole hub down, behind a yes/no. Imported from [issue #122](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/122).

Seen (operator, 2026-11-11): to stop everything on a machine without a reboot, the operator runs several verbs by hand:
`lym beam stop` for the orch and dobby of the prime and of each beam, `lym reed down` in each worktree for the tmux sessions, and `lym tender reap` for run processes no run owns.
It should be one simple action.

- A button in the reed status bar, shown only in the prime orch's session, that takes the whole hub down, after a yes/no confirmation.
- It ends the orch and dobby of the prime and of every beam, the reed sessions of the runs' worktrees, and run processes no run owns.
- Whether it first pauses the hub, so a run's turn is interrupted cleanly, and what the confirmation says, are open.
- The operator closes terminal windows (Konsole, the VS Code terminal) by hand.
- Built on the run FSM and its pause and cancel intents (operator, 2026-11-15), so a stop leaves every run in a pushed state another start or another machine goes on from.
  The adopt decision record kept a hub-wide pause machine-local; this button needs no shared pause between machines either.

### machine-restart-shortcut

One desktop launcher brings back every hub and beam that was in flight after a crash or reboot.

Seen (operator, 2026-11-08 and 2026-11-11): OSL-1046 and Neve crash often.
After a crash the operator finds every hub and project that was in flight, often three or four with beams under them, and starts each orch session by hand.
Once an orch is up, it and its dobby take the runs up again by themselves; a run whose step was cut off halts (`loop-exited`) and the orch settles it.
Finding what was running is the hard part, not resuming it.
VS Code reopens its own windows on Kubuntu.

- A `lym` verb starts again every project that was in flight on the machine: the hub prime and every live beam under it.
  It opens the hub's VS Code workspace file, `<hub>/<repo>.code-workspace`,
  and for the prime and each beam a terminal outside VS Code in the worktree running `lym s`, which starts its dobby and orch and attaches to its reed session.
  It opens no task window and resumes no run; the orchs and dobbies take the runs up.
- Desktop launchers call the verb: a `.desktop` file on Linux, a `.cmd` file on Windows.
  lym adds and removes them as hubs and beams come and go, and removes a hub's launcher when another machine takes the hub over.
- It starts only what this machine owns: it reads the owner of the hub's prime and of each beam, the owner `lym adopt` writes,
  and skips every one another machine owns, saying which machine holds it.
- Fixed by the operator: one launcher per hub plus one that starts every hub;
  beams are included; resuming interrupted runs is left to the orchs;
  nothing another machine owns is started; `.desktop` on Linux and `.cmd` on Windows, added and removed by lym.

entries.title: codexengine
entries.body:
## Goal (operator, 2026-11-03)

`codexengine` landed with project `codex-engine` and has run motif runs well, but was never tested as a whole.
A stress test proves, on real launches, that the engine does everything its design says, the hooks above all, and records each fault as a bug note.

## Codex parity (from the Sketch `codex-same-as-claude`, 2026-11-16)

A Codex session lym gives a role gets exactly what a Claude session in that role gets.
The tasks raddle filed from that Sketch build it:
`prompt-engine-per-launch`, `codex-standing-instructions`, `codex-wording-engine-blocks`, `codex-question-deny-nudge` and `launch-manifest-parity`.
The two projects `codex-engine-trial` and `codex-parity` were merged into this one (operator, 2026-11-16).

## What the engine is designed to do

The package doc `internal/shuttleengine/codexengine/doc.go` is the spec; each part below tests one area of it against real Codex sessions launched through `lym shuttle`.

1. Home and trust: the shared lym Codex home under `CODEX_HOME`, `auth.json` and sessions linked to the operator's home, `config.toml` rendered whole under a file lock, trusted roots for a worktree and a linked worktree, dropped roots for a gone folder, the read-back Warn, and the folder-trust prompt backstop.
2. Sandbox and refusals: `-a never -s workspace-write`, the records checkout as a writable root, a `.codex/rules` folder on disk, tracked by git or not, refusing the launch and a `.codex/config.toml` on disk named in a Warn (the checks read the folders on disk since `codex-trial-1-fixes`).
3. Hooks: SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, Stop with its reply, PermissionRequest and PostToolUse each reach the run's events file or activity stamp; an interrupt reads as interrupted through `turn_aborted`; the context size from `token_count`.
4. Shell guards: every installed guard row denies its command through the PreToolUse hook with its Codex steer, the prompt file carries the notices, and a hook that fails to run is seen failing open.
5. Pane and send: the composer, the busy line and the trust prompt read right; a long or multi-line send through the guarded paste-then-Enter lands whole; a dead pane after exit.
   Creel by the pane path, the only one a Codex strand has: a program's notice typed in full into an idle session, an agent's mail reminded with `run lym creel read`, and the Codex session running `lym creel read` and `lym creel post --reply` from inside its `workspace-write` sandbox, which must reach the creel daemon.
6. Skills: a `<plugin>:<name>` load reads the newest version's `SKILL.md` and the load is seen in the rollout; an unknown skill is reported unknown.
7. Stress: several Codex sessions at once, long sessions, repeated interrupts and sends, and a darn run with a Codex seat end to end.

## Rules

- Each part writes its findings to a report under `docs/research/`, and files each lym fault as a bug note on this board.
- Parts run as darn with profile `docs`, unless the operator says otherwise.
- A Codex run gets `high` effort at most.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-05)

Task `codex-creel-hooks` (`e3aedbc5`) gave Codex strands creel delivery through hooks, as Claude strands have: mail reaches a running session at the end of a tool call through `PostToolUse`, at a turn end through `Stop`, and an idle session through `codex queue` run by the strand's `hook-wait` waiter. So part 5's "the only one a Codex strand has" holds only for a strand opened without a prompt file (`OpenLaunch`, a standalone run), which stays a pane-mail strand.
Task `codex-creel-trial` (`afa2cf2e`, `docs/research/codex/engine-trial/codex-creel-trial-2026-11-05.md`) trialed it on real sessions in `lyt` and found one fault, filed as note `codex-idle-wake-extra-reminder`.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-07)

Task `codex-skill-load-false-missing` (`0e02aaad`) fixed a false `skill skipped ... cause="not loaded"` in part 6's load check.
`ClassifySkillLoad` now also reads a skill as loaded when a tool call output of the load turn holds the whole of its `SKILL.md`, so a seat that reads its skills through a path built at run time (a `cat .../skills/${name}/SKILL.md` loop) is no longer reported missing.
A partial output still leaves a skill missing.
The fix is checked against unit cases only: the original rollout and a live Codex run were not used, so part 6 should still see the load on a real session.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-08)

Task `codex-sandbox-mode` (`539525a0`) made part 2's sandbox a machine setting: `codex.yaml` has a `sandbox_mode` key, `workspace-write` by default or `danger-full-access`, set with `lym config codex --layer machine`.
A `danger-full-access` launch carries no sandbox flags, no network setting and no writable roots, and `OpenLaunch` does the same.
The change was checked by unit tests only.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-11)

Commit `9874c966` (task `codex-bubblewrap-sandbox`) added a third `sandbox_mode` value, `auto`, now the template default, so part 2 no longer needs the mode set by hand on a machine whose bubblewrap cannot start.
A launch under `auto` or `workspace-write` first probes the sandbox (`codex sandbox -c sandbox_mode="workspace-write" -- true` under the lym Codex home in the worktree):

- Under `auto`, a sandbox that starts runs `workspace-write`; one that refuses (OSL-1046's AppArmor-restricted user namespaces) runs `danger-full-access` with a warning naming bubblewrap's output.
- Under an explicit `workspace-write`, a sandbox that refuses refuses the launch, naming the cause and `lym config codex --layer machine --set sandbox_mode=auto`; the seat reads as not started, not stopped.
- `danger-full-access` runs no probe.

Both `Prepare` and `OpenLaunch` settle the mode through `launchSandboxMode` in `codexengine/sandbox.go`; `Prepare` refuses before `prompt.md` is written.
Part 2 therefore tests the probe, its three outcomes and the refusal on a real machine where bwrap fails (OSL-1046) and on one where it works (Neve), not only the fixed `workspace-write` flags.

entries.title: Review rounds converge: fixer rebuttals, incremental re-review, stalemate on no tree change
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-17)

Burler's review rounds circle more than they need to, in three ways.

- A fixer can fix a finding, leave it undone or defer it to the parent, but its argument against a finding never reaches the next round,
  so the reviewer can raise the same finding again on the same code.
- Each round after the first reviews the whole diff again, so it can raise new findings on code it passed before.
- A run's escalation cause `circling` (`internal/loomcli/circling.go`) is an LLM's judgment,
  though a round whose fix changes nothing in the warp tree is a stalemate a Go check can see.

Sources, from the survey F17 (`orchestrator-survey-ideas`):
ralphex's external review, where the agent fixes each finding or argues against it and the rebuttal goes into the next round,
and its `--review-patience=N`, which stops after N rounds with no tree change;
Traycer's re-verify, which checks only earlier findings and marks each resolved or outdated;
Fusion, which forbids new non-blocking findings on a re-review.

## Idea

- **Rebuttal.** The fixer may answer a finding with a rebuttal: why the code stands, with file and line.
  The next round's reviewer gets each rebuttal beside its finding and either withdraws the finding or answers the rebuttal.
  It applies to every reviewer engine, Codex included.
- **Incremental re-review.** A later round checks the earlier round's findings against the fixes and marks each resolved, still open or outdated.
  It raises a new finding only on code the fixes changed, and only at BLOCKING severity.
- **Stalemate on no tree change.** The Bouncer counts rounds whose fixer left the warp tree unchanged,
  and after a set number in a row halts the segment with a named stalemate cause before the bounce budget runs out.

entries.title: Record Codex edits for the edit-loop watch
entries.brief: Codex runs record no edits, so the edit-loop watch never notifies their parent
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-17)

The edit-loop watch from `edit-loop-detector` counts an agent's edits of one file and sends the run's parent a notice when they loop.
Only the claude engine implements `EditRecorder`: its sessions carry a PostToolUse hook on `Edit|Write` that records each edit.
A Codex run records no edits, so it never gets the notice.

## Idea

Give the codex engine an `EditRecorder` and an edit hook that records each file edit as the same slim line the claude engine writes,
so the engine-neutral watch in `internal/shuttleengine/editloop.go` covers Codex runs unchanged.
Codex edits files through its patch tool rather than `Edit` or `Write`,
so the hook reads the file paths from that tool's input; one patch touching several files records one edit per file.

entries.title: Edit-loop notices fire on a fixer editing one file
entries.brief: Fixers and one-document writers edit one file many times by design, so the edit-loop watch reports ordinary work as a loop
entries.body:
## Seen (orch, 2026-11-17)

The edit-loop watch landed in `c167e803` (four edits of one file within five minutes sends the parent a notice).
Within its first hour it sent two notices for `gate-test-map-mode`'s Plan-Burler-Fix agent,
which edited `_lym/plan/01-gate-test-map-mode.md` four times within five minutes each time.
That agent was applying the round-2 review's findings, one Edit per site, to the one plan file it owns; it was making progress.
Minutes later `codex-standing-instructions`' Code-Burler-Fix agent drew one for `instructionfiles.go`, fixing several findings in that file.
A fixer applying several findings to one file, or a writer whose whole output is one document,
edits that file many times by design, so the watch reads ordinary work as a loop.

## Idea

Count an edit toward a loop only when it undoes or repeats an earlier one,
for example the same `old_string` edited back and forth, or the file's content returning to an earlier hash,
instead of counting every edit of the file.
Failing that, exempt the roles whose output is one document, or give them a higher count.
